deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is part of Riemann's physiological manuscript on the mechanics of the middle ear. This draft corresponds to the posthumous paper 'Mechanik des Ohres', which I recall (not checked here) was edited by Henle and published in 1867 in Henle–Pfeufer's Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, and later included in the Gesammelte Werke.

The page has two parts.

(1) Conclusion of a methodological caveat from p.16. Riemann distinguishes the 'listening' ear from the 'non-listening' ear. In the listening ear, the tensor tympani pulls the stapes footplate slightly against the labyrinth fluid. The labyrinth pressure then slightly exceeds the tympanic-cavity pressure, and the solid parts of the ossicular chain are pressed against one another. He says one may doubt such a permanent tension, and suppose instead that ligaments and muscle tone accommodate the ossicles to temperature changes without mutual pressure. Even so, his analysis has shown that the exact interlocking of all parts is secured only under such pressure. His investigation therefore holds at least for the attentive ear, deliberately prepared for exact hearing. It remains possible that the (waking?) ear is permanently adapted, perhaps to a lesser degree.

(2) Start of a kinematic description of the ossicular apparatus as a rigid-body mechanism:
- The malleus and incus together form one body, rotatable about a fixed axis.
- Articulated with it is a piston, the stapes, which presses on the fluid of the oval window.
- One end of the rotation axis is the short process of the incus. It is fixed by the incudo-tympanic joint to the posterior wall of the tympanic cavity.
- The other end is the long (anterior) process of the malleus. It projects, surrounded only by soft tissue, into a fissure. Page 18 continues: the gap between the anterior-superior end of the tympanic ring and the petrous bone, lying in a groove of the ring (in the newborn).

In modern terms, this sets up a model of a rigid body with one rotational degree of freedom (a lever), coupled through a joint to a piston that drives an incompressible fluid. No equations of motion or lever ratios appear on this page.

results.what: Qualitative argument that firm contact of the ossicular joints requires a slight standing pressure (tensor tympani pressing the stapes into the labyrinth fluid), with the 'listening' ear as the case analysed
results.modern_name: Preloading/static tension of the ossicular chain; accommodation role of the middle-ear muscles
results.usually_credited_to: Discussed by 19th-century otologists and physiologists (Johannes Müller, Helmholtz 1868, Politzer); Riemann's version is in his published 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867)

results.what: Model of the ossicles as one rigid body (malleus + incus) rotating about a fixed axis (anterior malleal process to short incus process), articulated with a stapes piston
results.modern_name: Ossicular rotation axis / lever model of the middle ear
results.usually_credited_to: Axis concept in Henle's anatomy and elaborated by Helmholtz (1868); Riemann's posthumous 1867 paper gives the same description

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely anatomical and physiological description, with no mathematics. Its content is essentially the text of Riemann's already published posthumous paper 'Mechanik des Ohres', so nothing here is new or unattributed.
transcription_corrections: Line 'Das eine Ende der Umdrehungsaxe, der kurze Fortsatz': the manuscript reads 'Das eine Ende der Umdrehungsaxe, ist der kurze Fortsatz des Ambosses, ist mittelst ...'. The word 'ist' before 'der kurze Fortsatz' is present but omitted in the machine transcription; Riemann's own phrasing is redundant.

The struck-out opening words are not clearly 'Weiterhin gefunden'. They appear to be a cancelled variant such as 'wir weiter gefunden', duplicating the 'weil wir gefunden' at the end of p.16. The reading is uncertain.
'Ambos-Paukengelenks' is confirmed. The spelling 'Ambos' (single s) is used throughout, with 'Ambosses' in the genitive.
